##  Abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently hallucinate when external knowledge is absent, undermining reliability in high-stakes domains. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mitigates this by grounding responses in retrieved evidence, while Graph-based RAG (GraphRAG) encodes entities and relations as structured graphs to support multi-hop reasoning. However, prior studies report inconsistent gains over standard text retrieval, leaving unclear when GraphRAG is practically beneficial.We evaluate when GraphRAG provides measurable advantages over Text-RAG across three task families: factoid QA, multi-hop reasoning, and domain-specific factuality. We further analyze two system-level enhancements: Cache-Craft for inference efficiency and Corrective RAG (CRAG) for retrieval robustness. Unlike prior work focusing on isolated components or metrics, we present a controlled system-level comparison under identical model backbones, jointly measuring accuracy, latency, robustness, and cost.Results show that GraphRAG significantly improves multi-hop reasoning and domain factuality, but provides negligible gains for shallow factoid QA while introducing substantial latency and cost overhead. These findings provide clear, scenario-specific guidance on when structured retrieval is justified.

### I. Introduction
Large Language Models (LLMs) achieve strong performance across a wide range of language tasks but frequently generate hallucinations, producing fluent yet factually incorrect outputs that undermine reliability in high-stakes domains such as medicine, law, and finance [1]. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mitigates this issue by grounding model outputs in external retrieved evidence, improving factual consistency while remaining more efficient than long-context LLM approaches [2].
